citation.title: Nonparametric identification is not enough, but randomized controlled trials are

standing_assumptions:
Superpopulation setting: an i.i.d. sample with a binary outcome, a binary treatment and one continuous covariate; all probabilities and expectations are over repeated i.i.d. samples. Transcribed from the page images. Printed page = PDF page + 1 (Observational Studies 11.1 (2025): 3-16; PDF p. 1 is a cover sheet).

(S1) Sampling model, Section 2, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'We assume that we have an i.i.d. sample $(W_i, Y_i, X_i)$ from some large population, where $Y_i$ and $X_i$ are binary, and $W_i$ is drawn from a continuous distribution (either known or unknown). As above, $Y_i$ is the outcome, $X_i$ is the treatment, and $W_i$ is the covariate. We restrict our attention to simple treatment assignment mechanisms that assign treatments independently between units with unequal treatment probabilities that depend only on the unit’s own observed covariate $W_i$. We formalize this restriction as an unconfoundedness assumption, as stated below. The fact that the support of $W_i$ is large (here uncountable) is central to our discussion, because it ensures that all units will have unique covariate values.'

(S2) Consistency, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'For our discussion, we invoke the consistency assumption (c.f., the stable unit treatment value assumption), $Y_i = (1 - X_i)Y_i(0) + X_iY_i(1)$,'

(S3) Unconfoundedness, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'and unconfoundedness, $Y_i(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X_i \mid W_i, \quad \forall x \in \{0, 1\}$.'

(S4) Propensity score and positivity, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'We define the propensity score function as $\pi(w) = \Pr(X_i = 1|W_i = w)$, and assume that positivity holds, meaning that $\delta < \pi(W_i) < 1 - \delta$ with probability one for some positive $\delta$.'

(S5) Estimand, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'Without loss of generality, the parameter of interest is the average potential outcome under treatment: $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$.'

(S6) Known propensity score, p. 6 (PDF p. 5): 'In an RCT, all determinants of treatment are known because the experimenter decides how treatment is assigned. We assume full compliance with the treatment assignment and complete ascertainment of the outcome $Y_i$. This means that unconfoundedness holds by design, because the treatment assigned to unit $i$ only depends on its covariate $W_i$. Similarly, positivity can also be guaranteed to hold by design. [...] in an RCT, the propensity score function, $\pi(w)$, is known to the researcher, since it is specified by the experimental design.' Footnote 2, p. 6: 'We continue to maintain the assumption that the sample is i.i.d. to ensure comparability with the observational setting.' Propositions 2, 3 and 4 each open with 'Suppose the propensity scores are known.' Proposition 1 concerns the case in which $\pi$ is not known.

(S7) Estimators. Horvitz-Thompson, Proposition 2, p. 6 (PDF p. 5): $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$. Cross-fitted regression estimator, p. 7 (PDF p. 6): 'Let $s : [n] \to \{0, 1\}$ be a deterministic function that partitions the sample into two groups of roughly equal size, such as $s(i) = \lfloor (2i + n)/2n \rfloor$. Let $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ be two estimators of the regression function $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|W_i = w]$, where $\hat g_0$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 1\}$ and $\hat g_1$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 0\}$. The regression-based estimator of $\mu$ is then $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{X_i[Y_i - \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]}{\pi(W_i)} + \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)\right\}$.'

(S8) Notation that is not printed in the paper and is used in the targets below (the validators' notation; definitions, not extra assumptions): $m(w) = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i = w]$ (the paper writes this regression function out, p. 7); $F_W$, the distribution of $W_i$; $\mathbf{W} = (W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n)$ (printed, p. 16); $\mu_{\mathbf{W}} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} m(W_i)$; $q(w) = (1 - \pi(w))/\pi(w)$. The validators take the vectors $(W_i, Y_i(0), Y_i(1), X_i)$ to be i.i.d. across $i$ and the potential outcomes to be binary; the paper says only that $Y_i$ and $X_i$ are binary, and with consistency, unconfoundedness and positivity this gives $Y_i(1) \in \{0, 1\}$ almost surely, so $0 \le m(w) \le 1$. $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 6); proof in Appendix A, pp. 15-16 (PDF pp. 14-15)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] Proposition 3 Suppose the propensity scores are known. Then a finite-sample-valid $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is $\hat\mu \pm \sqrt{\xi \log(2/\alpha)/2n}$, where $\xi = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}$ is the mean of the square inverse of the propensity scores. [Text after the proposition, p. 7] 'The proposition follows directly from Hoeffding’s inequality, similar to the confidence interval described by Robins and Wasserman (2012a); we provide a proof in the appendix for completeness. This confidence interval is conservative relative to, for example, approaches based on normal approximations, but has the benefit of being finite-sample valid, therefore guaranteeing uniform validity. Note that the width of the interval decreases at the parametric rate $O(n^{-1/2})$.' [Proof as printed: Appendix A, pp. 15-16 (PDF pp. 14-15)] 'Proof [Proposition 3] The proposition states $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}\right) \le \alpha$. Let $\mathbf{W} = (W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n)$ be a vector collecting all covariates. By the law of total probability, we have $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}\right) = \mathrm{E}\left[\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n} \,\middle|\, \mathbf{W}\right)\right]$. The Horvitz–Thompson estimator can be written $\hat\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i$, where $A_i = [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$. Because the outcome is binary, the bound $0 \le A_i \le [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}$ holds with probability one. Recall that $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mu$, so by Hoeffding’s inequality, $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n} \,\middle|\, \mathbf{W}\right) \le 2\exp\left(\frac{-2\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}[n\pi(W_i)]^{-2}}\right)$. Recall that $\xi = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}$, allowing us to write the right-hand side as $2\exp\left(\frac{-\left\{n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}\right\}\log(2/\alpha)}{n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}}\right) = 2\exp\Big(-\log(2/\alpha)\Big) = \alpha$.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Estimator: Proposition 2, p. 6 (PDF p. 5)] $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$. [$\xi$: Proposition 3, p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] $\xi = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}$, a random variable (a function of the sampled covariates). [Estimand: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$, the population mean. [Finite-sample valid: p. 7 (PDF p. 6), the sentence before the proposition] 'This confidence interval is finite-sample valid, meaning that its coverage is guaranteed to be greater or equal to its nominal level even in small samples.' Coverage is over repeated i.i.d. samples (S1); Appendix A (p. 15, PDF p. 14) restates the claim as $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}\right) \le \alpha$. [Radius] The root covers the whole expression $\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n$, in which $/2n$ is division by $2n$ (the last display of the proof rewrites $-2\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n$ as $-\{n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}\}\log(2/\alpha)$) and $\log$ is the natural logarithm (the proof uses $2\exp(-\log(2/\alpha)) = \alpha$). [Level] The paper states no restriction on $\alpha$; the validators read the claim for every $0 < \alpha < 1$ and every $n \ge 1$. [Propensity score, positivity, consistency, unconfoundedness: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] as in the standing assumptions (S2)-(S4). [Summands and covariate vector: Appendix A, p. 16 (PDF p. 15)] $A_i = [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$, $\mathbf{W} = (W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n)$.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, listed because P046-E001 is rated Moderate. It is false as printed for unrestricted $\alpha$: P046-T1 gives a law satisfying every standing assumption with $n = 100$ and $\alpha = 10^{-7}$ in which the noncoverage probability exceeds $\alpha$, and P046-T2 shows that the conditional Hoeffding display of the proof fails (the conditional mean of $\hat\mu$ given $\mathbf{W}$ is $\mu_{\mathbf{W}} = n^{-1}\sum_i m(W_i)$, not $\mu$). The corrected statement is P046-T3. Steps of the printed proof that are correct: the law of total probability display (valid because $\xi$ is a function of $\mathbf{W}$), the representation $\hat\mu = \sum_i A_i$ with $0 \le A_i \le [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mu$, and the algebra of the last display. What is not established by the audit: undercoverage of the printed interval at 95%, 99% or any conventional level (in the design of P046-T1 the exact noncoverage is below $\alpha$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ and $0.01$), or invalidity for every $\alpha$. A case in which the printed statement holds (v2 derivation.md section 7): if the propensity score is constant, $\pi(W_i) = p$, then $\xi = p^{-2}$ is deterministic and unconditional Hoeffding for $X_iY_i/p \in [0, p^{-1}]$ gives exactly the printed radius. The abstract's claim that knowledge of the propensity score yields 'finite-sample valid confidence intervals that shrink at a parametric rate' (p. 3, PDF p. 2) survives through P046-T3. The source the paper cites for a similar interval (Robins and Wasserman 2012a) uses the deterministic bound $\delta$ in place of $\xi$ (external check recorded under P046-N001); that is the alternative form in P046-T3.

canonical_claim.location: p. 6 (PDF p. 5); supporting sentence on p. 7 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 6 (PDF p. 5)] Proposition 2 Suppose the propensity scores are known. Then the Horvitz–Thompson estimator $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$ is unbiased, uniformly root-n consistent, and asymptotically normal for $\mu$. [Text after the proposition, p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] 'The proposition follows directly from the law of iterated expectations, along with standard results for the sample mean. The proposition requires that the outcome distribution is well behaved, which is ensured when the outcome is binary; separate moment conditions are necessary to extend the proposition to general outcomes.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Estimand: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$. [Propensity score and positivity: p. 5] $\pi(w) = \Pr(X_i = 1|W_i = w)$, $\delta < \pi(W_i) < 1 - \delta$ with probability one for some positive $\delta$. [Standing assumptions: p. 5] i.i.d. sample, binary $Y_i$ and $X_i$, consistency $Y_i = (1 - X_i)Y_i(0) + X_iY_i(1)$, unconfoundedness $Y_i(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X_i \mid W_i$. [Unbiased] $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mu$ for every $n \ge 1$; this is the exact finite-sample part. [Uniformly root-n consistent] Not defined in the paper. The introduction (p. 5, PDF p. 4) speaks of 'good (unbiased and uniformly root-$n$ consistent) estimators and inferential procedures', and p. 6 (PDF p. 5) says 'The focus on uniform consistency allows the population distribution to depend on $n$.' The reading used by the audit's readers: for the class $\mathcal{P}_\delta$ of laws satisfying (S1)-(S4) with a common positivity constant $\delta$, $\lim_{M \to \infty}\sup_{n}\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}_\delta} P\left(\sqrt{n}\,|\hat\mu - \mu(P)| > M\right) = 0$. The paper states positivity 'for some positive $\delta$' and does not say that $\delta$ is common to the class; without a common $\delta$ the variance bound below is not uniform. [Asymptotically normal] Not defined further in the paper; read as: for each fixed law, $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, \sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2 = \mathrm{Var}(X_iY_i/\pi(W_i)) = \mathrm{E}[m(W_i)/\pi(W_i)] - \mu^2$ (a point mass if $\sigma^2 = 0$), $m(w) = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i = w]$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for every $n \ge 1$ and every law satisfying (S1)-(S5). (i) [Printed, as the first display of the proof of Proposition 4(a), p. 16 (PDF p. 15)] $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{X_iY_i(1)}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{E}[X_iY_i(1) \mid W_i]}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i]\,\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i]}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$, 'where the first equality uses the law of iterated expectations, the second equality uses unconfoundedness, and third equality uses the fact that $\mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i = w] = \pi(w)$'; with $X_iY_i = X_iY_i(1)$ (consistency) this gives $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mu$. The proof of Proposition 3 (p. 16) also uses 'Recall that $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mu$'. (ii) [Printed in the proof of Proposition 3, p. 16, in the form $0 \le A_i \le [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}$] $0 \le X_iY_i/\pi(W_i) \le 1/\pi(W_i) < 1/\delta$. (iii) [Not printed; the audit readers' derivation] $\mathrm{E}\left[(X_iY_i/\pi(W_i))^2\right] = \mathrm{E}[m(W_i)/\pi(W_i)]$, so $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu) = \frac{1}{n}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{m(W_i)}{\pi(W_i)}\right] - \mu^2\right) \le \frac{1}{n\delta}$ (also $\le \frac{1}{4n\delta^2}$, from the range in (ii)). (iv) [Not printed] Chebyshev: $\Pr\left(\sqrt{n}\,|\hat\mu - \mu| > M\right) \le \frac{1}{\delta M^2}$ for every $n$ and every law with positivity constant $\delta$, which is the uniform root-n statement in the reading above. The remaining limit step is the i.i.d. central limit theorem for the bounded summands $X_iY_i/\pi(W_i)$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P046-H2; both fresh readers found that it holds (candidates.json: held_up). One printed proposition with an exact finite-sample part (unbiasedness; hence priority 3) and two asymptotic parts (uniform root-n consistency, asymptotic normality), for which (i)-(iv) are the finite lemmas. The paper prints no proof beyond the sentence quoted; the conditional-mean calculation is also written out in the validator artifact named here (section 1: $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu \mid \mathbf{W}] = \mu_{\mathbf{W}}$ and $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mu$). The formal readings of 'uniformly root-n consistent' and 'asymptotically normal' in definitions_needed are the readers', not the paper's. In the paper's three simulated data generating processes $m = \pi$, so $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu) = \frac{3}{4n}$ exactly (readers' check; not part of the target).

canonical_claim.location: p. 8 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix A, p. 16 (PDF p. 15)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 8 (PDF p. 7)] Proposition 4 Suppose the propensity scores are known. Then: (a) $\hat\mu_R$ is finite-sample unbiased for $\mu$. [Proof as printed: Appendix A, p. 16 (PDF p. 15)] 'Proof [Proposition 4(a)] Write the estimator as $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{X_iY_i(1)}{\pi(W_i)} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{X_i\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)}{\pi(W_i)} + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)$. Focusing on the expectation of the individual terms, we have $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{X_iY_i(1)}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{E}[X_iY_i(1) \mid W_i]}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i]\,\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i]}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$, where the first equality uses the law of iterated expectations, the second equality uses unconfoundedness, and third equality uses the fact that $\mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i = w] = \pi(w)$. Following a similar pattern, we have $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{X_i\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i]\,\mathrm{E}[\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i) \mid W_i]}{\pi(W_i)}\right] = \mathrm{E}[\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]$. We have $\mathrm{E}[X_i\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i) \mid W_i] = \mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i]\,\mathrm{E}[\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i) \mid W_i]$ because of the use of cross-fitting in the construction of $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$, meaning that $X_i$ is independent of $\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)$ conditional on $W_i$. The expectation of the third set of terms is $\mathrm{E}[\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]$, matching the second set of terms, so they cancel. We can therefore conclude that $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_R] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)] = \mu$.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Cross-fitted estimator: p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] 'Let $s : [n] \to \{0, 1\}$ be a deterministic function that partitions the sample into two groups of roughly equal size, such as $s(i) = \lfloor (2i + n)/2n \rfloor$. Let $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ be two estimators of the regression function $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|W_i = w]$, where $\hat g_0$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 1\}$ and $\hat g_1$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 0\}$. The regression-based estimator of $\mu$ is then $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{X_i[Y_i - \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]}{\pi(W_i)} + \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)\right\}$.' So the function $\hat g_{s(i)}$ applied to unit $i$ is computed from the observations of the other group only, and is therefore independent of $(W_i, X_i, Y_i)$ under i.i.d. sampling. [Finite-sample unbiased] $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_R] = \mu$ for every $n$ and every such pair of estimators; the proposition places no condition on $\hat g_0$, $\hat g_1$ (they may be misspecified; p. 7: 'the adjusted estimator will remain finite-sample unbiased even if the model is misspecified'). [Estimand, propensity score, positivity, consistency, unconfoundedness: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] as in (S1)-(S5). The first display of the printed proof uses $X_iY_i = X_iY_i(1)$, which is consistency (S2).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P046-H4, part (a); an exact finite-sample statement with a printed proof, which both fresh readers followed equality by equality and found correct. No finding touches part (a). A condition the proof uses without printing it (fresh reader's note): the expectations $\mathrm{E}[\hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]$ must exist, that is, the fitted values must be integrable; and the fits must be functions of the other group's observations alone (or of those and randomness independent of unit $i$). The paper's remark on p. 8: 'All parts of Proposition 4 are previously known results. For completeness, we provide a proof for Proposition 4(a) in the appendix.'

canonical_claim.statement: [p. 8 (PDF p. 7)] Proposition 4 Suppose the propensity scores are known. Then: [...] (b) If $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ are convergent in mean square (but not necessarily consistent for the true outcome regression function), then $\hat\mu_R$ is root-n consistent for $\mu$. [...] (d) If $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ are consistent for the true regression function, then $\hat\mu_R$ attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. [Text after the proposition, p. 8] 'All parts of Proposition 4 are previously known results. For completeness, we provide a proof for Proposition 4(a) in the appendix. See van der Vaart (1998) for Proposition 4(b). See Section 3 of Cao et al. (2009) for Proposition 4(c); see also Rubin and van der Laan (2008). See Theorem 5.1 in Chernozhukov et al. (2018) for Proposition 4(d). Note that in (b), we do not require that $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ converge to the true regression function, or to any other particular function, only that they converge to some functions.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Cross-fitted estimator: p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] $s : [n] \to \{0, 1\}$ a deterministic function that partitions the sample into two groups of roughly equal size, such as $s(i) = \lfloor (2i + n)/2n \rfloor$; $\hat g_0$ estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 1\}$ and $\hat g_1$ using $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 0\}$; $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{X_i[Y_i - \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]}{\pi(W_i)} + \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)\right\}$. [True regression function: p. 7] $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|W_i = w]$, written $m(w)$ below. [Convergent in mean square, part (b)] Not defined further in the paper; with the remark on p. 8 ('only that they converge to some functions'), read as: there are fixed functions $g_0, g_1$ with $\|\hat g_j - g_j\|_{L^2(F_W)} \to 0$ (in mean square, hence in probability) as $n \to \infty$, $j = 0, 1$. [Root-n consistent] Not defined in the paper; read as $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu_R - \mu) = O_p(1)$. [Consistent for the true regression function, part (d)] Not defined in the paper; read by the validators, with part (b) as context, as $\|\hat g_j - m\|_{L^2(F_W)} \to 0$ in probability, $j = 0, 1$. [The semiparametric efficiency bound, part (d)] Not written out in the paper. The doubt check for P046-E003 settled that the citation the paper attaches to part (d) (Theorem 5.1 of Chernozhukov et al. 2018, whose last sentence names 'the semi-parametric efficiency bound of Hahn (1998)') identifies it as the bound for $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)]$ in the model with known $\pi$ and unrestricted covariate distribution, which on the scale of $n$ times variance is $B_H = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{m(W)(1 - m(W))}{\pi(W)}\right] + \mathrm{Var}(m(W))$; 'attains' is read as $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu_R - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, B_H)$. [Asymptotic sequence] Not specified in the paper; $n \to \infty$ under a fixed law satisfying (S1)-(S5). [Standing assumptions: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] (S1)-(S5).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: All exact for a fixed law satisfying (S1)-(S5) and fixed $n$; none is printed in the paper (parts (b) and (d) are stated by citation). Derived in the validator artifact named here (the doubt check of P046-E003: derivation.md, sections 2-3 and 5.1) and, for (a), also in runs/P046/validate/P046-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 5 and 7. Write $I_j = \{i : s(i) = j\}$, $n_j = |I_j|$, $\sigma_1^2(w) = m(w)(1 - m(w))$, and for a fixed function $g$, $A_g = X[Y - g(W)]/\pi(W) + g(W)$. (a) $\mathrm{E}[A_g] = \mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(A_g) = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\sigma_1^2(W)}{\pi(W)}\right] + \mathrm{Var}(m(W)) + \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1 - \pi(W)}{\pi(W)}(m(W) - g(W))^2\right]$; at $g = m$ this is $B_H$, and under positivity the last term vanishes only if $g = m$ almost surely. (b) Exact decomposition, for fixed functions $g_0, g_1$ and $e_j = \hat g_j - g_j$: $\hat\mu_R - \mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sum_{i \in I_j}(A_{g_j,i} - \mu) + R_0 + R_1$ with $R_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I_j}\left(1 - \frac{X_i}{\pi(W_i)}\right)e_j(W_i)$; with $g_0 = g_1 = m$ the leading term is $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\phi_H(O_i)$, $\phi_H = \frac{X(Y - m(W))}{\pi(W)} + m(W) - \mu$, which has mean zero and variance $B_H$. (c) Conditional on the training fold of $\hat g_j$, the observations in $I_j$ are i.i.d. and independent of $e_j$; $\mathrm{E}[1 - X/\pi(W) \mid W] = 0$ and $\mathrm{E}[(1 - X/\pi(W))^2 \mid W] = (1 - \pi(W))/\pi(W)$, so $\mathrm{E}[R_j \mid \text{training}_j] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\sqrt{n}R_j \mid \text{training}_j) = \frac{n_j}{n}\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1 - \pi(W)}{\pi(W)}e_j(W)^2\right] \le \frac{n_j}{n\delta}\|e_j\|_{L^2(F_W)}^2$. (d) Conditional Chebyshev: for $\epsilon, \eta > 0$, $\Pr(|\sqrt{n}R_j| > \epsilon) \le \Pr(\|e_j\|_2^2 > \eta) + \frac{\eta}{\delta\epsilon^2}$. The limit steps resting on these: $R_j = o_p(n^{-1/2})$ when $\|e_j\|_2 \to 0$ in probability; the central limit theorem for the bounded independent summands of the leading term; for part (d), the identification of $B_H$ as the efficiency bound (the canonical gradient $\phi_H$, derivation.md section 2), which is semiparametric theory and not a finite lemma.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P046-H4, parts (b) and (d): asymptotic statements that the paper gives by citation and without proof (p. 8); the fresh readers and the validators derived them under the readings in definitions_needed and found that they hold. Part (c) is not in this target: it is false as printed (P046-E002; counterexample P046-T4, corrected statement P046-T5). P046-E003 concerns part (d) and is rated a clarity note, not an error: the set-up allows the covariate distribution to be 'either known or unknown' (p. 5), and in the smaller model with a known covariate distribution the efficiency bound is $B_K = \mathrm{E}[m(W)(1 - m(W))/\pi(W)]$, lower than $B_H$ by $\mathrm{Var}(m(W))$, which the printed estimator does not attain unless $m(W)$ is constant (validator's exact example: $n$-scaled variance $11/24$ against $3/8$). The doubt check settled that part (d) names the Hahn bound $B_H$, which $\hat\mu_R$ attains under $L^2$-consistent cross-fitting whether or not the covariate distribution is known; the known-distribution comparison belongs to a claim the paper does not make and is not a target. In part (b) the two folds may converge to different functions $g_0 \ne g_1$. The pinpoint citations (van der Vaart 1998; Theorem 5.1 of Chernozhukov et al. 2018) were checked only as far as recorded under P046-N001 (undetermined). The identification of $B_H$ as the efficiency bound is semiparametric theory; the finite lemmas (a)-(d) are the exact content on which the two limit statements rest.

canonical_claim.statement: [p. 6 (PDF p. 5)] Proposition 1 Suppose we have a study for which consistency, unconfoundedness, and positivity hold. Without further assumptions, there exists no estimator of $\mu$ that is uniformly consistent. [Sentence introducing the proposition, p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] 'A central result of Robins–Ritov (Theorem 3 in their paper) implies that we cannot estimate this quantity well in an observational study without imposing additional assumptions, as described by the following proposition.' [Text after the proposition, p. 6] 'The Robins–Ritov proof involves an adversarially constructed distribution at each $n$, with increasingly small bins as the sample size grows. In particular, with high probability, no bin includes two or more observations, so the within-bin correlation between propensity scores and outcomes cannot be estimated from the data. The focus on uniform consistency allows the population distribution to depend on $n$.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Setting: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] An i.i.d. sample $(W_i, Y_i, X_i)$, $Y_i$ and $X_i$ binary, $W_i$ drawn from a continuous distribution (either known or unknown); consistency $Y_i = (1 - X_i)Y_i(0) + X_iY_i(1)$; unconfoundedness $Y_i(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X_i \mid W_i$, $\forall x \in \{0, 1\}$; $\pi(w) = \Pr(X_i = 1|W_i = w)$ with positivity $\delta < \pi(W_i) < 1 - \delta$ with probability one for some positive $\delta$; $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$. In this proposition the propensity score function is not known to the analyst (the contrast with Propositions 2-4, which open 'Suppose the propensity scores are known'). [Estimator] Not defined in the paper; read as a sequence of measurable functions $\hat\mu_n$ of the observed sample $(W_i, Y_i, X_i)_{i=1}^{n}$. [Uniformly consistent] Not defined in the paper; the paper's gloss is 'The focus on uniform consistency allows the population distribution to depend on $n$' (p. 6). The standard reading used by the audit's readers: over a model $\mathcal{P}$ of laws, for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} P\left(|\hat\mu_n - \mu(P)| > \epsilon\right) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. [Without further assumptions] $\mathcal{P}$ is the set of all laws satisfying (S1)-(S4), with no restriction on the outcome regression $m(w) = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i = w]$ or on the propensity score function beyond positivity. The proposition then says: for every estimator sequence there is $\epsilon > 0$ with $\limsup_{n}\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} P\left(|\hat\mu_n - \mu(P)| > \epsilon\right) > 0$. The readers' construction below proves this already on the smaller class with $W_i \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$ known and a common positivity constant $\delta < 1/4$, which implies it for $\mathcal{P}$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The paper prints no proof; it attributes the result to Theorem 3 of Robins and Ritov (1997), which is not among the staged sources (pinpoint undetermined, P046-N001). The finite steps below are the lower-bound construction that one of the audit's fresh readers verified (summarized in candidates.json under P046-H1; written out in that reader's notes, runs/P046/fresh-sol/notes.md, which is outside the validators' folder, so the construction is given here in full); they are not printed in the paper and have no validator artifact. Fix $n$ and a number of bins $K$; partition $(0, 1)$ into $K$ intervals of equal length; let $W_i \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and $Y_i(0) = 0$ in every law, with $X_i$ and $Y_i(1)$ conditionally independent given $W_i$. Law A: $\pi(w) = 1/2$ and $m(w) = 1/2$ for all $w$, so $\mu_A = 1/2$. Laws $B_\tau$, $\tau \in \{1, 2\}^K$: in a bin of type 1, $(\pi, m) = (1/4, 1)$; in a bin of type 2, $(\pi, m) = (3/4, 1/3)$; so $\mu_{B_\tau} = \frac{1}{K}\left(\#\{j : \tau_j = 1\} + \frac{1}{3}\#\{j : \tau_j = 2\}\right)$. All these laws satisfy (S1)-(S4) with any common $\delta < 1/4$. (a) Single-bin observable law: if the type of a bin is drawn with probability $1/2$ each, an observation in that bin has $\Pr(X = 1, Y = 1) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot 1 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{4}$, $\Pr(X = 1, Y = 0) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot 0 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\Pr(X = 0) = \frac{1}{2}$ (with $Y = 0$), the same three probabilities as under law A. (b) Collision bound: the probability that two or more of the $n$ covariates fall in a common bin is at most $\frac{n(n - 1)}{2K}$. (c) Indistinguishability: when the types $\tau_j$ are independent and equiprobable, the mixture over $\tau$ of the laws of the sample under $B_\tau$ coincides with the law of the sample under A on the event that no bin contains two or more observations; hence the total variation distance between the two laws of the sample is at most $\frac{n(n - 1)}{2K}$, which tends to zero for $K = n^3$. (d) Separation: under the equiprobable prior, $\mathrm{E}[\mu_{B_\tau}] = \frac{2}{3}$, so $\mu_{B_\tau}$ concentrates at $2/3$ as $K \to \infty$, at distance $1/6$ from $\mu_A = 1/2$. The limit step resting on these (two-point, or Le Cam, argument, not written out by the reader): an estimator that is uniformly consistent would be within $\epsilon < 1/12$ of $1/2$ with probability tending to one under A and within $\epsilon$ of $\mu_{B_\tau}$, hence near $2/3$, with probability tending to one under the mixture, which (c) forbids. A variant by the other reader uses bin types $(\pi, m) \in \{(1/10, 1/10), (9/10, 9/10)\}$ against $\pi = 1/2$, $m = 82/100$ ($\mu = 1/2$ against $82/100$); its bin types are those of the paper's third simulated data generating process (p. 9, PDF p. 8: $100n$ bins with $\Pr(Y_i(1) = 1 \mid W_i = w) = \Pr(X_i = 1 \mid W_i = w)$ equal to $1/10$ if $B(w) = \lceil 100nw \rceil$ is odd and $9/10$ if it is even), which the paper says 'resembles the adversarial functions constructed in the proofs by Robins–Ritov'.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P046-H1; both fresh readers found that the proposition holds as stated for the unrestricted model (held_up_with_caveat: the caveat concerns the abstract, not the proposition). The proposition is asymptotic and is given by citation, so the Lean statement can be stated faithfully and its finite lemmas (a)-(b) proved; the formal reading of 'uniformly consistent' is the readers', not the paper's. P046-E004 (a clarity note, not an error) concerns the abstract's wording of this result (p. 3, PDF p. 2: no uniformly consistent estimator 'unless the propensity score is known or additional assumptions are made on the complexity of the propensity score function'): restrictions on the outcome regression alone can also give a uniformly consistent estimator, as the body acknowledges (p. 6); the validator's exact outcome-only example imposes a restriction that Proposition 1 excludes, so it is not a counterexample to the proposition and is not a target. The abstract states the result for 'the average treatment effect'; the proposition is for $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$ ('Without loss of generality', p. 5). Whether Theorem 3 of Robins and Ritov (1997) is the result that implies the proposition could not be checked (P046-N001, undetermined).
